doc.title: Yusef Lateef — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Road bands and the Gillespie band
title: The serious attitude of musicians on the bandstand
summary: Lateef answers Jackson on the seriousness of the late-1940s musicians, comparing playing to acting and thinking as well as feeling.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Sure. I want to go back to something...
Yeah.
...you mentioned earlier concerning uh the demeanor of musicians during this period.
Oh yeah.

Do you think that uh...looking again at the broader perspective, was this kind of part of the changing social firmament? Because you hear a lot about musicians say, as you mentioned, being more serious on the band stand as opposed to–and and I don’t want, I’m not saying this to be disparaging, but–uh as opposed to a more overtly amiable person like, say Louis Armstrong.
Mmhmm.

And and uh as you know there seem, there seems to have been just a more serious presentation of the music, people like Dexter Gordon, as you’ve mentioned. Do you, as I said, do you think that’s part of uh something that was in the air in music, or, and beyond that, or, or uh...?
Well, I don’t know if I understand the question clearly

Well, just a more serious attitude uh...maybe on the part of, of African- Americans, in general, you know, we’re looking at the late ‘40s. I don’t know, maybe, maybe that’s, you don’t think that’s the case at all, but...
Yeah, well, I think the predominate attitude was that of seriousness. Uh...like uh Ted Dunbar...the late...
Guitarist.

...guitarist. He...he said that, “the bandstand is a serious place.” Um, the late Eddie Harris said uh, “music is as serious as a heart attack.” Um, and that’s what I sensed being in the presence of people like um Sonny, the late Sonny Stitt, um...and Paul Chambers...Coleman Hawkins and Charlie Parker. It was, this is a serious affair uh...and that was the attitude that prevailed: of seriousness. No tomfoolery as this definition of, of the music as been given by Merriam-Webster CD-ROM. They define the music as tomfoolery, skullduggery–it’s none of that. It’s a serious event. And uh...when we’d, during that period when musicians would get on the bandstand, you could feel the seriousness, as though gladiators were–not to kill anyone–but the attitude was to be expressive...heartfelt, mind-embedded expressions. Uh that’s what they meant by “telling a story.”
Mmhmm.
Um...it’s, it’s as serious as um–there’s a school of acting, for example. The school of drama was express by people like uh...um who was the gentleman with the bald head? He played Moses.
Uh...Charlton Heston, I think, but he not–
No.
Oh, Yul Brynner.
Yul Brynner, yeah.
Okay. He was, he was Pharaoh actually. Yeah. Right.
Yeah. Pharoah, yeah. Uh...there’s a school of acting. I can’t think of it.
Was it, was it Stanislavski, or was it the method acting? I know there were a couple of schools around that time.
Yeah, the old lady who used to sit on the, the wagon in the [indecipherable] pictures.
Oh, I know who you mean. I can’t, I can’t recall her name.
Yeah. Anyway, they would use uh mental imagery.
Mmhmm.

Like, if they want to express sadness uh they would focus on a grandparent who had passed, at that moment and, of course, tears would roll down their cheeks. And, of course, those observing would feel the sadness. The music was as serious as that in many instances. Not only sadness: happiness...all the emotional, psychological states that man can experience were expressed in the music. Uh the musicians felt deeply, and thought intensely. It’s not just playing what you feel. It’s playing what you feel plus what you think. It’s not a non-thinking occupation.

I know that Duke Ellington would say there is–someone asked him about “serious music” and he said, there’s no person serious than, more serious than a uh–and he, of course, as most of us disdain the “jazz” word–he said, “There’s no more serious musician than someone who plays this music,” and...
Yes.
